title: Automated Analysis of IntelliCage-based Mouse Experiments
author: Hindermann, Daguano Gastaldi, et al.

steps.title: House mice before experiment
steps.instruction: Group‑house mice (up to 16 per type IV cage, 20.5 × 55 × 38.5 cm) from weaning (PND 21) in stable groups; maintain ~50 % humidity, ~22 °C, 12 h light‑dark cycle, with water and food ad libitum; use wood‑chip bedding (~3 L) covering the floor but avoid bedding in the four conditioning corners.

steps.title: Place RFID transponder (injector method)
steps.instruction: Implant a disposable sub‑cutaneous RFID transponder using a pre‑filled injector.

substeps.instruction: Prepare the work area with anesthesia setup, ethanol, cotton pads, forceps, injector with needle, transponder, scanner, eye‑protection salve and a heating pad set to ~37 °C.
Place a clean home cage on the heating pad.
Record the transponder ID from the package together with the mouse ID and load the transponder into the injector.
Anesthetize the mouse (e.g., Avertin or Ketamine) and position it on its belly; apply eye‑protection salve.
Disinfect the neck skin with an ethanol‑soaked cotton pad.
Lift the neck skin with forceps and inject the transponder sub‑cutaneously.
Scan the newly placed transponder and verify that the ID matches the recorded note.
Terminate anesthesia and return the mouse to its new home cage.
CRITICAL: The whole procedure takes ~30 s per mouse; check transponder presence before experiments.

steps.title: Place RFID transponder (incision method)
steps.instruction: Implant a reusable RFID transponder via a small neck incision and suture.

substeps.instruction: Prepare the work area with anesthesia setup, ethanol, cotton pads, forceps, scissors, bulb‑headed probe, polypropylene 3‑0 suture, transponder, scanner, eye‑protection salve and a heating pad (~37 °C).
Place a clean home cage on the heating pad.
Place the transponder in a small dish with Ringer solution or buffer and scan its ID, noting it with the mouse ID.
Anesthetize the mouse (e.g., Avertin or Ketamine) and position it on its belly; apply eye‑protection salve.
Disinfect the neck skin with an ethanol‑soaked cotton pad.
Make a ~3 mm incision in the neck skin with scissors.
Create a small sub‑muscular pocket with the bulb‑headed probe and insert the transponder.
Scan the transponder to confirm correct ID.
Close the incision with polypropylene 3‑0 suture.
Terminate anesthesia and return the mouse to its new home cage.
CRITICAL: This method may take up to 5 min per mouse.

steps.title: Create experimental design file
steps.instruction: Prepare the IntelliCage experiment designer file with animal information and dummy transponder.

substeps.instruction: Download IntelliR from https://github.com/vgastaldi/IntelliR to obtain required files.
Open the experimental designer file (e.g., “challenge1.experiment”) with IntelliCagePlus Designer.
Select “Animals” and enter each mouse’s ID as “Name” and its transponder ID as “Tag”.
Assign each animal to a group (A‑D) in the “Group” column (e.g., “Group1A”).
Assign each animal to a corner (1‑4) in the “Cluster” column.
Optionally add notes such as the specific IntelliCage system; sex and body weight are not required.
Add one “dummy” animal per IntelliCage system using a non‑implanted transponder ID to enable system testing.
Save the file and transfer it to the computer that controls the IntelliCage(s).
CRITICAL: Transponder IDs must be entered completely and correctly; corner assignments should be randomized and balanced.

steps.title: Prepare IntelliCage hardware
steps.instruction: Clean the IntelliCage, verify door mechanisms, and run a Demo Mode test.

substeps.instruction: Wear gloves and clean the entire IntelliCage thoroughly with 70 % ethanol.
Manually check all door mechanisms for smooth, quiet movement; if a door is noisy or blocked, disassemble, clean and re‑assemble it.
Start the IntelliCagePlus Controller software.
Run “Demo Mode” for at least 12 h (ideally 24 h) to test all functions.
Synchronize the computer clock with the light/dark cycle time switches.
After stopping Demo Mode, inspect the system report for any error indications; proceed only if none are reported.

steps.title: Load and start experimental file
steps.instruction: Load the prepared experiment into the controller and verify corner functions.

substeps.instruction: In IntelliCagePlus Controller, load the experimental file (e.g., “challenge2.experiment”).
Click the “Start” button to launch the experiment.
Insert the dummy transponder (or your index finger) into each corner tube to generate a “visit” (green “Presence” rectangle).
When presence is detected, gently tap both operant walls; the screen should flash the “Nosepoke” indicator for that corner.
After the door opens, gently tap the water‑bottle tip; the screen should flash the “Lick” indicator.
Repeat the visit‑nosepoke‑lick test for all four corners, both doors and bottles.
If presence is not registered, warm your hand (cold hands may fail); if “Lick” does not flash, remove the glove and try again.
Click the “Stop” button to end the test session.

steps.title: Set up IntelliCage cage
steps.instruction: Install the IntelliCage into the housing cage and add bedding, food, water and enrichment.

substeps.instruction: Gently lower the IntelliCage into a large type IV cage, checking cable connections and avoiding jams.
Add ~3 L of wood‑chip bedding (or equivalent) to cover the floor, keeping the conditioning corners free of bedding.
Add standard food pellets; ensure multiple layers so lower pellets are pinned by the upper layer.
Place the food houses (e.g., 4 × red triangular mouse houses, ACRE011, Tecniplast) beneath the feed rack so mice can reach them.
Fill the water bottles and test them by gently tapping the tip.
Add enrichment items (mouse houses, wood‑chip bedding); avoid paper nesting material or items that can be dragged into conditioning corners.

steps.title: Install R and RStudio
steps.instruction: Install the R programming environment and optional IDE.

substeps.instruction: Download R from the CRAN mirrors page https://cran.r-project.org/mirrors.html (IntelliR tested with R 4.3.0‑4.4.3).
Follow the on‑screen installer instructions for your operating system.
Optionally download RStudio (version 2024.12.1+563, “Sky” theme) from https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/ and install it.

steps.title: Download and set up IntelliR
steps.instruction: Obtain the IntelliR scripts and prepare the required folder hierarchy.

substeps.instruction: Download IntelliR from its GitHub page https://github.com/vgastaldi/IntelliR (originally archived at DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14912687).
Create a main folder (e.g., “IC files”). Inside it, create a project subfolder (e.g., “longDTA”) and a results subfolder (e.g., “results”).
Place all IntelliCage output ZIP files from the experiment into the project folder, preserving the example structure provided in the downloaded “IC files”.
Create an unblinding file named <project>.txt in the root of the main folder; it must be tab‑separated with two columns headed “ID” and “Group”, matching the IDs used in the IntelliCage.

steps.title: Run IntelliR analysis
steps.instruction: Execute the IntelliR pipeline via RStudio or command line.

substeps.instruction: Extract the downloaded ZIP file; locate the script “initial_intellicages.R”.
Open the script in RStudio and click the “Source” button (or run via Rscript). A Shiny page will open in the default browser.

On the Shiny page, fill in all required fields: select the project folder, upload the unblinding file, and choose the appropriate processing script for your OS (processing_intellicages_windows.R or processing_intellicages_unix.R).
Choose colors for groups using standard R color names or hex codes; specify the number of groups (2‑4).
Click the “Click to confirm” button to start analysis (≈10 min).
CRITICAL: Windows users may encounter button‑click issues; see troubleshooting problem 8 if this occurs.
After completion, a new folder named after your project will appear in the results directory, containing processed data files and automatically generated figures.

description: The increasing demand on behavioral research on mice in combination with challenges of established behavior tests in regard to excessive handling, social isolation as well as testing the animals during their resting phase, led to the development of the IntelliCage (TSE Systems, Berlin, Germany),2 a well-established system, also previously utilized in our group.2,3,4 Fitting into a standard Makrolon type IV rodent cage (20.5 × 55 × 38.5 cm), the system allows housing of up to 16 mice, enabling behavioral testing within a social and therefore stress-reduced context. Regarding the spatial requirements per mouse, please check your local regulatories. The system consists of four computer-controlled operant training chambers, one in each corner of the cage. Mice are able to enter each operant chamber through a tube which is equipped with a radio-frequency identification (RFID) antenna, individually identifying the visiting animal by the afore implanted transponder. Within each chamber, there are two operant conditioning walls, each equipped with sensor beams close to the surface, enabling the detection of a visiting mouse’s nosepoke. In the center of each operant conditioning wall is a computer-controlled door, giving access to the tip of a water bottle behind it. Furthermore, each bottle is equipped with a “lickometer”, measuring the individual number of licks. Additionally, there are three light emitting diodes (LEDs) above each door which can be individually controlled, allowing computer-controlled display of light in three different intensities and four colors (red, blue, green, yellow). Each operant conditioning chamber also contains an outlet to deliver air-puffs as aversive stimuli, which can be delivered at up to 2 bar, depending on your valves settings.5 The three basic parameters on mouse behavior provided by the IntelliCage system are visits (RFID & presence in tube), nosepokes (sensor beams, operant wall), and licks (liquid consumption, tip of bottles).
